transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The Trump administration has less than half an hour now to comply with a court-ordered
deadline to respond to three major news organizations who filed a notice of non-compliance.
As NPR's David Fochenflick explains, CNN, Politico and MSNow say their journalists were
again blocked from entering the White House today, hours after a federal judge issued
a temporary restraining order that the White House lift its ban on the outlets.
CNN, Politico and MSNow said some of the staffers were denied entry to the White House early
this morning.
Politico said one of its reporters had their press pass confiscated by the Secret Service,
was blocked from entering the White House grounds.
You saw On the Air live this morning on CNN that one of their White House journalist Betsy
Klein was turned back, although the network says one of its producers was able to enter
using their pass.
I've spoken to folks at CNN and MSNow and what they're saying at the moment is they're
not 100% clear.
Is this intentional foot-dragging, an intention to defy, or just logistical complications?
NPR's David Fochenflick reporting in court yesterday the media organizations argued President
Trump violated their constitutional rights in stripping them of their White House credentials
because he didn't like their coverage of them.
The Justice Department cites national security concerns in defense of Trump's actions.
The legal battle affects White House television pool coverage of President Trump's high stakes
meeting with China's visiting leader Xi Jinping.
As NPR's Emily Feng reports, Iran, trade and the future of artificial intelligence are
on the two leader's agenda.
Trump and Xi will hold bilateral meetings on tariffs and the war on Iran.
The two countries are trying to maintain what China calls "strategic stability," a dayton
in the relationship.
And just before the meetings this week, the U.S. announced a two-month extension of a
trade truce that lets it access Chinese-made rare-earth products.
But other sources of tension remain, including new Chinese actions designed to block U.S.
sanctions and recent U.S. legal actions against importing and selling Chinese drones and internet
routers.
Emily Feng, NPR News, Washington.
The Navy says eight sailors attempted suicide during the 10-month tour of the USS Abraham
Lincoln carrier group, Morphman Piers Quill Lawrence.
Family members of U.S. sailors first warned about conditions on the aircraft carrier during
what became a modern record for days at sea.
At the time, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth dismissed the reports, and President Trump
said the ship's tour had been, quote, "not nearly long enough."
But in a letter responding to New York Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, the Navy revealed that
eight sailors had attempted suicide during the deployment, including one who jumped overboard.
Gillibrand accused the president of treating the sailors with open disrespect.
CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper has said that the Lincoln had a relatively low rate
of mental health cases, but acknowledged the stress of such a long time at sea.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988.
You're listening to NPR.
Mortgage rates are at their highest levels since January of 2025.
The finance giant Freddie Mac reports the average rate for a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage
topped 7 percent this week.
Rates on the 15-year loan, widely popular with those seeking to refinance, have also
risen.
Rates have generally increased over the last six months and added hundreds of dollars to
the monthly cost of a new home loan.
The Federal Reserve has said the U.S. war with Iran has helped elevate inflation, and
the Fed recently raised interest rates in response for the first time in three years.
Congress's prime minister is renewing his calls for Britain to return the Parthenon
marbles.
They've been the focus of Greek-British negotiations for years.
We have more on this from NPR's Lauren Frere.
In a Guardian newspaper op-ed, the Greek prime minister says there is political will for
the return of the Parthenon marbles, which are also sometimes called the Elgin marbles,
named after Lord Elgin, who had them chiseled off the Parthenon more than 200 years ago.
They're currently on display in the British Museum in London.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsutakos compares the marbles to the Bayou tapestry, which France
returned to England for the first time in more than 900 years.
But unlike the tapestry, which is back only on loan, Mitsutakos says Greece will not borrow
its own antiquities.
And he says that just as Britain would never cut the tapestry in two, the marbles should
not be separated, as they currently are, about half in London, half in Athens.
Lauren Frere, NPR News, London.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News in Washington.
If the creation of the universe was translated into music, what would it sound like?
Ideas about how to make sense of the incomprehensible.
Most of science in general is actually intuitable.

CNN, Politico and MSNow journalists blocked from White House despite federal judge's temporary restraining order
President Trump meets with China's Xi Jinping to discuss tariffs, Iran, and artificial intelligence
Eight sailors attempted suicide during USS Abraham Lincoln's 10-month deployment, Navy reveals to senator
Mortgage rates reach highest levels since January 2025, averaging above 7 percent for 30-year loans
